intro: The finale of Mozart’s last symphony opens with four slow notes, C–D–F–E, and in its closing pages five separate tunes are played together. Bruno Walter conducts the Columbia Symphony Orchestra.

cues.title: Opening four-note theme, first violins
cues.text: The first violins play C–D–F–E in long notes, with quicker figures around them. Other string parts soon take up the four-note phrase. Mozart later inverts it and sets other themes above it.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, opening theme and imitative continuation. K. Dawn Grapes discusses the themes’ contrapuntal treatment: https://fcsymphony.org/mozart-41-jupiter/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dated 10 August 1788, Vienna
cues.text: Mozart dated this symphony 10 August 1788. The E♭ and G minor symphonies had preceded it that summer. For this C major orchestra he added the trumpets and timpani that the G minor symphony leaves out.
cues.evidence: Date and scoring in the work records for K. 550 and K. 551: https://imslp.org/wiki/Symphony_No.41_in_C_major,_K.551_(Mozart,_Wolfgang_Amadeus) and https://imslp.org/wiki/Symphony_No.40_in_G_minor,_K.550_(Mozart,_Wolfgang_Amadeus).

cues.title: Development, bars 158–224
cues.text: In the development, bars 158–224, the themes pass between parts and through changing keys. A new entry can begin underneath one already in progress. The four long notes sound against running figures in the strings.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, development, bars 158–224.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recapitulation in C major
cues.text: At bar 225 the violins bring back the opening theme in C major above moving inner strings. The other parts enter against it and overlap it.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, recapitulation from bar 225.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Michael Puchberg, 1788
cues.text: In Vienna on 27 June 1788 Mozart wrote to Michael Puchberg asking for a longer loan. He said his new rooms were cheaper and that he was working hard, but his bills kept outstripping him. He closed the appeal with “I shall be silent and hope.”
cues.evidence: Mozart to Michael Puchberg, 27 June 1788, Bauer–Deutsch 1079. Our translation of “schweigen und hoffen”: https://dme.mozarteum.at/DME/objs/raradocs/transcr/pdf/BD_1079.pdf.

cues.title: Coda, five themes combined
cues.text: The coda first inverts the four-note idea in a quieter passage. Mozart then combines five themes in counterpoint, each with its own rhythm, in long notes, running figures and short replies.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 357–404. The five-theme combination is described by K. Dawn Grapes, Fort Collins Symphony: https://fcsymphony.org/mozart-41-jupiter/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing C major cadences
cues.text: The running lines converge on the final C major cadences. Trumpets and timpani join the winds and strings in the closing chords.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 405–424.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: From exposition to development
transitions.from: A · Four notes in the violins
transitions.to: Dev · Four notes passed between instruments
transitions.how: The exposition closes with a cadence in G major. The development opens at a lower dynamic, and the strings carry familiar figures into new keys. Entries overlap and are repeated at different pitches, moving the harmony away from G major.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 151–169.

transitions.title: Dominant pedal into the recapitulation
transitions.from: Dev · Four notes passed between instruments
transitions.to: A′ · Opening theme in C major, violins
transitions.how: The development comes to rest on the dominant of C major, with G held in the bass. Above the moving inner strings, the violins bring back C–D–F–E in long notes in the home key, and the accompaniment keeps up its quick pulse.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 219–233.

transitions.title: Inversion of the four-note theme
transitions.from: A′ · Opening theme in C major, violins
transitions.to: Coda · Five themes combined in counterpoint
transitions.how: A C major close leads into the coda at bar 357. From bar 361 a quieter passage follows, with the four-note theme inverted in sustained notes. From bar 372 the strings start the final contrapuntal combination over these notes and add the quicker themes one at a time. The full orchestra then confirms C major.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), IV, bars 355–383: coda from bar 357, inversion from bar 361, contrapuntal combination from bar 372.

source.title: Mozart, Symphony No. 41, Breitkopf & Härtel, Mozarts Werke VIII/41 (1880), numbered public-domain scan
source.locator: IV. Molto allegro, PDF pp. 35–56, bars 1–424: four-note theme, development, return and contrapuntal coda.

timeline.note: First violins play C–D–F–E above moving second violins; lower strings join as the phrase expands.
The full orchestra answers, with trumpets and timpani reinforcing the strings.
Strings begin the development above held horn notes; woodwinds rejoin as the phrases continue.
Woodwinds and strings pass the themes between them, punctuated by horns, trumpets and timpani.
The opening theme returns above moving inner strings; winds, brass and timpani join its continuation.
Full orchestral phrases alternate with lighter passages for strings and winds.
The full orchestra plays a phrase at the start of the coda, then stops.
Strings and flute hold long notes that play the four-note theme in inversion.
The themes combine in the strings, with winds, brass and timpani joining the final build.

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to play the finale through. The work was K. 466 in D minor. It opens with syncopated strings, and the piano enters with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert excellent.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart later dedicated the quartets to him.
